title: input types: search, tel, url, range, color, file, hidden
learningObjectives: Explain input types: search, tel, url, range, color, file, hidden and build forms with appropriate native HTML behaviour.

understand.concept: HTML input types communicate the expected data and provide browser-specific controls and validation. search, tel, url, range, color, file, and hidden each have different purposes. A tel input does not validate a telephone number format automatically, while url has built-in URL constraint validation.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing a suitable input type improves keyboard layouts, browser affordances, and validation. File inputs require careful handling of selected files and server-side checks; hidden fields are not trusted security controls.
understand.analogy: Input types are specialised tools: choose the one that matches the user's task rather than treating every field as plain text.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; actual form submission and validation follow HTML algorithms and browser behaviour.

explain.narrative: The browser provides different controls for search, URL, telephone, range, colour, and file selection. The hidden field is not displayed but can still be modified by the user.

examples.code: <form><label>Search <input type='search' name='q'></label><label>Website <input type='url' name='site'></label><label>Phone <input type='tel' name='phone' inputmode='tel'></label><label>Range <input type='range' name='level' min='0' max='10'></label><label>Colour <input type='color' name='theme'></label><label>File <input type='file' name='attachment' accept='.pdf,image/*'></label><input type='hidden' name='formVersion' value='1'></form>
examples.explanation: The browser provides different controls for search, URL, telephone, range, colour, and file selection. The hidden field is not displayed but can still be modified by the user.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered form demonstrating the HTML form behaviour described.

practise.guidedTask: Build a form with at least four of these input types. Explain which types provide native validation and which require additional application rules.
practise.independentTask: Build an accessible form using appropriate input types, names, labels, and constraints. Inspect the submitted FormData and explain which controls are successful.
hints: Give every user-facing control a visible label.
Do not trust hidden fields or client-side validation for security.
Test keyboard and mobile input behaviour.

questions.prompt: Does type='tel' automatically validate a telephone number format?
questions.explanation: tel provides a telephone-oriented input but does not impose a universal phone-number format.

questions.prompt: What is a good form-design principle?
options: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.answer: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.explanation: Accessible forms use appropriate controls and labels, while security validation belongs on the server.
